sources.title: Photosynthesis (encyclopedia entry)
sources.excerpt: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy - typically from sunlight - into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism. The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting. Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds, typically carbohydrates like sugars, starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose. When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration.

sources.title: Cellular respiration (encyclopedia entry)
sources.excerpt: Cellular respiration is the process of oxidizing biological fuels using an inorganic electron acceptor, such as oxygen, to drive production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which stores chemical energy in a biologically accessible form. Cellular respiration may be described as a set of metabolic reactions and processes that take place in the cells to transfer chemical energy from nutrients to ATP, with the flow of electrons to an electron acceptor, and then release waste products.

sources.title: Photorespiration (encyclopedia entry)
sources.excerpt: Photorespiration (also known as the oxidative photosynthetic carbon cycle or C2 cycle) refers to a process in plant metabolism where the enzyme RuBisCO oxygenates ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), wasting some of the energy produced by photosynthesis. The desired reaction is the addition of carbon dioxide to RuBP (carboxylation), a key step in the Calvin-Benson cycle, but approximately 25% of reactions by RuBisCO instead add oxygen to RuBP (oxygenation), creating a product that cannot be used within the Calvin-Benson cycle. This process lowers the efficiency of photosynthesis, potentially lowering photosynthetic output by 25% in C3 plants. Photorespiration involves a complex network of enzyme reactions that exchange metabolites between chloroplasts, leaf peroxisomes and mitochondria.

representations.audience: a reader with no background in biology
representations.statement: Photosynthesis is how green plants use light energy to build sugars out of carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product. The sugars are the plant's stored food.
representations.scope: A first account, suitable for a school-level explanation. It describes what happens, not the machinery.
assumptions: The reader knows what a gas is and what light is.
The plant is green and growing in light.
includedFacts: Light energy is the input.
Carbon dioxide and water are the inputs.
Sugars are the output.
Oxygen is released.
omitted: That the oxygen comes from water rather than from the carbon dioxide.
That the plant also respires, at the same time.
That the reaction is split into light-dependent and light-independent stages.
That RuBisCO can react with oxygen as well as carbon dioxide.
validityConditions: An introductory account of the overall balance, not of the mechanism.

representations.audience: a reader who has finished an introductory biology course
representations.statement: Photosynthesis has two linked stages. The light-dependent reactions, in the thylakoid membranes, harvest light, split water and build a proton gradient that drives ATP and NADPH production. The light-independent reactions, in the chloroplast stroma, use that ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into carbohydrate through the Calvin-Benson cycle. The plant also runs cellular respiration to release that stored energy again, and it does so continuously, including in daylight.
representations.scope: The two-stage structure and the parallel respiration, without molecular detail.
assumptions: The reader can accept a compartment structure: thylakoid membrane and stroma.
Chloroplasts and mitochondria are distinct compartments.
includedFacts: The light-dependent reactions build ATP and NADPH and split water.
The Calvin-Benson cycle fixes carbon dioxide using ATP and NADPH.
Respiration runs in parallel with photosynthesis.
Photorespiration is a competing reaction at RuBisCO.
omitted: The Z-scheme of electron transport.
The chemical identity of the proton gradient.
The three-carbon and two-carbon intermediates of the C2 cycle.
The anatomical difference between C3 and C4 leaves.
validityConditions: Suited to reasoning about why a change in light, carbon dioxide or temperature alters the outcome.

representations.audience: an undergraduate student of plant physiology
representations.statement: Photosynthetic performance is the net result of a chain of competing processes rather than a single reaction. Light harvesting by the light-harvesting complexes feeds the photosystems; electron transport establishes a proton gradient whose yield sets the rate of ATP and NADPH formation; RuBisCO catalyses carboxylation but also oxygenation, and the oxygenation route is paid for through photorespiration, which returns carbon dioxide to the chloroplast only after a cycle spanning chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion. Diffusion to the carboxylation site, through the stomata and the mesophyll, is itself a major limitation, and in angiosperms the biochemical, stomatal and mesophyll limitations are close to balanced.
representations.scope: The limiting processes and how they trade against one another.
assumptions: The reader knows the Calvin-Benson cycle and can follow the C2 cycle.
Stomatal and mesophyll conductance are treated as the diffusion terms.
includedFacts: RuBisCO oxygenation diverts carbon into photorespiration.
Photorespiration spans three organelles.
Stomatal conductance responds to light, carbon dioxide and water.
In angiosperms the limitations are well balanced.
omitted: The photosynthetic apparatus of C4 and CAM plants in detail.
The specific engineering attempts to improve crop photosynthesis.
validityConditions: C3 plants, steady state, non-stress conditions.
The balance statement does not hold under severe stress.

representations.audience: a researcher or an advanced student
representations.statement: Oxygenic photosynthesis couples a membrane protonmotive force to a carbon fixation cycle. Photosystem II absorbs photons through the light-harvesting complex II and uses the excitation energy to extract electrons from water; the resulting oxygen is the by-product of that extraction. The electrons pass through the photosynthetic electron transport chain, protons are pumped across the thylakoid membrane, and the resulting gradient drives ATP synthase. NADPH is formed on the stromal side. In the stroma, ATP and NADPH are spent by the Calvin-Benson cycle, in which RuBisCO adds CO2 to RuBP, and the product is reduced to triose phosphate. When RuBisCO instead oxygenates RuBP, the two-carbon product is routed through the peroxisome and the mitochondrion and carbon dioxide is released; carbon is thereby lost and ATP and reducing power are consumed without carbon being fixed.
representations.scope: The coupled mechanism, with the chemical steps that can be drawn on paper.
assumptions: The reader is comfortable with a proton gradient and with enzyme catalysis.
Oxygenic phototrophs with a Calvin-Benson cycle.
includedFacts: Water is the electron donor in photosystem II, and oxygen is its by-product.
The proton gradient across the thylakoid drives ATP synthesis.
RuBisCO catalyses both carboxylation and oxygenation of RuBP.
Photorespiration releases carbon dioxide and consumes energy.
omitted: The chemistry of photosystem I.
The regulation of RuBisCO activity by RuBisCO activase and inhibitors.
The carbon-concentrating anatomy of C4 and CAM plants.
validityConditions: Assumes steady-state conditions; the oxygenase/carboxylase ratio is temperature and carbon dioxide dependent.

representations.audience: a reader with no background in biology
representations.statement: Cellular respiration breaks down food molecules to release the energy a cell can use. It needs an electron acceptor, usually oxygen, and it produces ATP.
representations.scope: What respiration is for and what it needs.
includedFacts: Respiration releases energy from food.
Oxygen is the usual electron acceptor.
ATP is the usable energy currency.
omitted: That plants carry it out as well as animals.
That it runs at the same time as photosynthesis.

representations.audience: a reader who has finished an introductory biology course
representations.statement: Cellular respiration is a set of reactions in which the energy in nutrients is transferred to ATP by moving electrons to an inorganic electron acceptor, typically oxygen, and releasing waste products. It runs continuously in plant cells, including during daylight, so a plant both makes sugar by photosynthesis and spends it by respiration.
representations.scope: The transfer of energy to ATP, and the fact that plants respire continuously.
assumptions: The reader knows that ATP is the cell's usable energy currency.
includedFacts: Electron flow to an acceptor drives ATP production.
Waste products are released.
Plants respire during daylight as well as at night.
omitted: The individual reactions of the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain.
The stoichiometry of ATP per glucose.

representations.audience: a reader with no background in biology
representations.statement: Photorespiration is a wasteful side reaction of photosynthesis: the plant's main carbon-fixing enzyme grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, and the plant has to spend energy undoing the result.
representations.scope: The idea of a competing, costly reaction, without the chemistry.
assumptions: The reader knows that photosynthesis fixes carbon dioxide.
includedFacts: The main enzyme can react with oxygen instead of carbon dioxide.
The side route costs the plant energy.
omitted: The approximate fraction of reactions.
The organelles involved.
Why it is worse in hot, dry conditions.

representations.audience: an undergraduate student of plant physiology
representations.statement: Photorespiration is the C2 oxidative photosynthetic carbon cycle. When RuBisCO oxygenates RuBP, a two-carbon product is formed that the Calvin-Benson cycle cannot use. The plant recovers it by moving it through the peroxisome and the mitochondrion, where glycine is converted to serine, carbon dioxide is released and ammonia is reassimilated. Because carbon dioxide is released again and ATP and reducing power were spent, photorespiration lowers net photosynthetic output; the fraction of RuBisCO reactions that take the oxygenation route is roughly a quarter in typical C3 conditions.
representations.scope: The pathway and its carbon and energy cost.
assumptions: The reader knows the Calvin-Benson cycle and the chemistry of amino acids.
includedFacts: The photorespiratory cycle spans chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion.
Carbon dioxide is released back to the chloroplast.
Roughly a quarter of RuBisCO reactions are oxygenations.
omitted: Engineering of photorespiratory bypasses.
The photorespiratory role in stress signalling.
validityConditions: C3 plants under typical conditions; the fraction varies with temperature and carbon dioxide.

representations.audience: a reader who has finished an introductory biology course
representations.statement: RuBisCO is the enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide, adding it to a five-carbon sugar to start the Calvin-Benson cycle. It is also the enzyme's weakness: it can add oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, and that mistake costs the plant energy.
representations.scope: The dual activity of one enzyme, and why it matters.
assumptions: The reader knows what an enzyme does.
includedFacts: RuBisCO catalyses carboxylation.
It catalyses oxygenation instead, about a quarter of the time.
The oxygenation route is the photorespiratory pathway.
omitted: The activation cycle and RuBisCO activase.
The evolutionary history of the enzyme.

representations.audience: an undergraduate student of plant physiology
representations.statement: The Calvin-Benson cycle fixes carbon dioxide in the stroma using ATP and NADPH from the light reactions. RuBisCO adds carbon dioxide to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate; the product is reduced and rearranged to regenerate the acceptor, so the cycle turns over continuously. The rate at which the cycle can run is set by the supply of ATP and NADPH and by the carboxylation rate of RuBisCO.
representations.scope: The cycle's inputs, its turning point and what limits it.
assumptions: The reader knows the products of the light reactions.
includedFacts: ATP and NADPH are consumed.
RuBP is the acceptor and is regenerated.
RuBisCO catalyses the fixation step.
omitted: Each named intermediate of the cycle.
The regulation of cycle enzymes.
validityConditions: Oxygenic phototrophs with a Calvin-Benson cycle.

representations.audience: an undergraduate student of plant physiology
representations.statement: The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membrane. Light-harvesting complex II transfers excitation energy to the photosystem II core, which extracts electrons from water; the electrons pass through the electron transport chain, protons are moved into the thylakoid lumen, and the gradient drives ATP synthase. The system must also dissipate excess excitation as heat, because unbalanced absorption produces damaging reactive oxygen species. Activation of RuBisCO lags when a shaded leaf is suddenly exposed to strong light, and that lag alone has been estimated to cut wheat assimilation by about a fifth.
representations.scope: The energetic machinery and its main costs.
assumptions: The reader knows the components of the thylakoid membrane.
includedFacts: LHCII transfers energy to the photosystem II core.
Water is split and the gradient drives ATP synthesis.
Excess light must be dissipated to avoid reactive oxygen species.
RuBisCO activation lags after a shade-to-sun transition.
omitted: The Z-scheme in detail.
Chlorophyll fluorescence measurement methods.
validityConditions: The 21% figure is an estimate for wheat.

representations.audience: a reader who has finished an introductory biology course
representations.statement: Stomata are adjustable pores in the leaf through which carbon dioxide enters and water vapour leaves. Stomatal conductance measures how freely gas moves through them. It responds to light, to the carbon dioxide concentration and to the plant's water supply, so closing the stomata to conserve water also restricts the carbon dioxide supply for photosynthesis.
representations.scope: The diffusion step and the trade-off it expresses.
assumptions: The reader knows that photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide.
includedFacts: Stomata control gas exchange.
Light, carbon dioxide and water supply affect conductance.
Conserving water by closing stomata restricts carbon dioxide uptake.
omitted: The hormonal signalling that opens and closes the stomata.
The mesophyll conductance component.
validityConditions: Leaf gas exchange in vascular plants.

representations.audience: an undergraduate student of plant physiology
representations.statement: A carbon-concentrating mechanism raises the carbon dioxide concentration around RuBisCO above the atmospheric level, which favours carboxylation over oxygenation. C4 plants achieve at least a tenfold concentration. Cyanobacteria that carry carboxysomes achieve up to one hundredfold, and the green alga Chlamydomonas, which carries pyrenoids, up to fortyfold. The strategies differ in the organelle that performs the concentration, but they serve the same purpose.
representations.scope: The purpose of the concentrating mechanisms and the magnitude of their effect.
assumptions: The reader knows why carboxylation and oxygenation compete.
includedFacts: Concentrating CO2 favours carboxylation.
C4 achieves at least tenfold.
Carboxysomes achieve up to one hundredfold; pyrenoids up to fortyfold.
omitted: The anatomical and biochemical detail of the C4 cycle.
Engineering these mechanisms into C3 crops.
validityConditions: The mechanisms as they occur naturally.

prerequisites.note: The fixation step is catalysed by RuBisCO, so the cycle cannot be explained without it.
Photorespiration begins at the oxygenation reaction of RuBisCO.
The photorespiratory cycle exists because the oxygenation product cannot enter the Calvin-Benson cycle.
The point of concentrating CO2 is to change the balance of the two reactions RuBisCO performs.
The light reactions are one half of photosynthesis.

revisions.summary: The introductory account was replaced by a two-stage account that adds respiration and the photorespiratory competition, and then by the limiting-process account.
addedFacts: The light-dependent reactions build ATP and NADPH and split water.
Respiration runs in parallel with photosynthesis.
Photorespiration competes with carboxylation at RuBisCO.
The biochemical, stomatal and mesophyll limitations are well balanced in angiosperms.
stillValid: Carbon dioxide and water are the inputs.
Sugars are the output and oxygen is released.
noLongerValid: That photosynthesis and respiration happen at different times of day.
That the released oxygen comes from the absorbed carbon dioxide.
That the account is complete without the respiration that consumes the sugar it produces.
newlyExplained: Why a plant in darkness still consumes oxygen.
Why raising carbon dioxide increases growth even though light is unchanged.
Why a hot, dry day can slow photosynthesis despite adequate light.
